newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels trap Zairean troops at Lubumbashi airport.
newsitem.headline: Rebels trap Zairean troops at Lubumbashi airport.

text.p: A showdown loomed on Thursday between rebels who consolidated control of Lubumbashi and diehard government troops who were trapped at the airport and had threatening to rain rockets on Zaire's second city.
A day after the rebel takeover, residents looted army premises and torched a military base at a presidential villa, but Laurent Kabila's forces slowly established order.

Expatriate sources said at least 100 troops from President Mobutu Sese Seko's elite DSP unit, minus most of the top brass who had fled bt air during the night, were holding the airport six km (four miles) northeast of the city, with as many rebels heading in their direction.
"We hope the DSP will not carry out their threat to fire their Stalin's Organs (rockets) on the city," said a longtime resident with high contacts.

Army generals, desperate to flee but initially without fuel to fly out on aircraft that braved the fighting to fetch them, had threatened on Wednesday night to fire rockets on the city into which the victorious rebels had marched just hours earlier.

A group of Belgian expatriates had carried out a daring late-night operation through the front line to get fuel to the airport in a truck with no lights, the sources said, and two planes took off into the dark for the capital Kinshasa.
Inexplicably, one left apparently empty and the second only a quarter full, with just 25 people on aboard.

General Molamba Bin Lowa, the army number one for Shaba province who had urged his men to fight to the end, was believed to have been among the officers onboard. It was unclear if any planes were left at the airport.

Wednesday's heavy artillery, mortar and machinegun fire calmed overnight but resumed intermittently in the morning. However, by noon (1000 GMT) there was no sound from the airport area which rebels had closed in on from all sides.
Disciplined columns of Kabila's forces marched into Zaire's copper capital and economic powerhouse on Wednesday morning.
The army largely melted away or changed sides, although some of an estimated 450 DSP troops in the city fought street battles as they retreated. There were some casualties.
A wave of joy swept the city of a million people who had said they were waiting impatiently to be liberated from Mobutu's corrupt and chaotic 32-year rule.
The chant of "Kabila, Kabila," rose from the city all day, while masses stripped military headquarters and the homes of generals and Mobutu's relatives of everything but the walls.
There was looting of shops in the city centre overnight and some residents said several bodies in the streets were looters shot by rebel soldiers. This could not be confirmed.
The free-for-all at the army bases and nearby military farmland resumed before dawn. One man was dragged down the street by a fierce guard dog he looted as people laughed.
At Mobutu's villa on the southern edge of town, people removed everything including chandeliers, wiring, carpets, doors and the kitchen sink. Whatever was left was smashed.
Army uniforms, rifles and unused ammunition littered floors flooded after sinks and toilets were ripped out.
Smoke and flames poured from buildings in the grounds used by the DSP as a store for ammunition, which exploded in the fire.

Elsewhere, signs of the passed Mobutu era -- the only one many people had known -- were swiftly eradicated. Obligatory portraits were burned and a monument to his MPR party pulled to the ground by a jeering mob.
